stories.summary: Além de criar animações, a ferramenta permite ajustar a velocidade de reprodução, editar quadros individuais e compartilhar o resultado O post ChatGPT ganha ferramenta para criar e editar GIFs apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

sources.name: Olhar Digital IA
sources.title: ChatGPT ganha ferramenta para criar e editar GIFs
sources.text: O ChatGPT ganhou novidade que pode facilitar a criação de conteúdo para redes sociais: a capacidade de produzir GIFs animados diretamente na plataforma. Com a atualização, usuários podem descrever a animação desejada em um comando de texto ou enviar uma fotografia para transformá-la em conteúdo animado. A novidade acompanha o lançamento do Images 2.6, nova versão do gerador de imagens da OpenAI . Além de criar animações, a ferramenta permite ajustar a velocidade de reprodução, editar quadros individuais e compartilhar o resultado. Até então, o ChatGPT não oferecia maneira nativa de produzir GIFs em uma única etapa. Era necessário recorrer a ferramentas externas ou realizar procedimentos adicionais para transformar imagens em animações. A OpenAI demonstrou o recurso com um comando simples: pedir ao chatbot que criasse um GIF de um gato dançando. O sistema produz a animação e oferece controles para modificar sua velocidade e visualizar os quadros que compõem o resultado. A atualização também contempla desenvolvedores. A OpenAI apresentou duas opções de modelos para geração de imagens por meio da API: As duas opções ampliam as possibilidades de integração da tecnologia em aplicativos e outros serviços digitais. O Images 2.6 está sendo disponibilizado para usuários do ChatGPT e do Codex nas versões web, desktop e aplicativos para dispositivos móveis. A distribuição ocorre de maneira gradual, portanto, a novidade pode não aparecer simultaneamente para todas as contas. Com a possibilidade de criar e editar animações diretamente no chatbot, a OpenAI amplia o alcance de suas ferramentas visuais. O recurso pode ser útil para produzir memes, ilustrações animadas, materiais de divulgação e conteúdos para redes sociais sem precisar alternar entre diferentes aplicativos. A mudança também reforça a estratégia da empresa de transformar o ChatGPT em plataforma de criação de conteúdo, indo além das tradicionais conversas por texto. Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

sources.title: ChatGPT agora cria GIFs com o nova IA Images 2.6
sources.text: Dots x Muse: Qual o Melhor Agente de IA em 2026? Dots da OpenAI ou Muse da Meta: qual ecossistema de agentes de IA vale mais a pena?. Crédito: Pedro Castro A OpenAI anunciou, na quarta-feira (4), o Images 2.6, novo modelo de geração de imagens do ChatGPT. Além de gerar imagens com maior velocidade, a nova inteligência artificial pode criar GIFs sem precisar de ferramentas adicionais. O Images 2.6 da OpenAI traz melhorias na velocidade de geração e no controle das criações . Segundo a empresa, a tecnologia produz imagens 50% mais rápido do que as versões anteriores e oferece maior precisão durante as edições. Na API, o novo modelo está disponível em duas versões: o GPT-Image-2.6 Flare é projetado para criar imagens mais rapidamente, priorizando a velocidade; o GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst, por sua vez, é voltado para trabalhos que exigem maior nível de detalhes, precisão e consistência entre edições. Segundo a OpenAI, os usuários já criam mais de 4 bilhões de imagens por semana no ChatGPT, Codex e API , superando os 3 bilhões semanais reportados anteriormente. A atualização também dá ao ChatGPT a capacidade de criar GIFs nativamente , sem depender de ferramentas externas. A IA gera uma sequência de imagens para proporcionar a sensação de movimento, permitindo ao usuário ajustar a velocidade da animação e editar quadros individuais após a produção. O Images 2.6 foi liberado globalmente no ChatGPT e no Codex, nas versões web, desktop e mobile, para todos os planos. Os modelos GPT-Image-2.6 Flare e Sunburst também estão disponíveis na API da OpenAI. Quer ficar por dentro das novidades do mundo da tecnologia? sources.title: ChatGPT agora cria GIFs animados direto no chat e permite editar quadros
sources.text: O ChatGPT ganhou um recurso nativo para criar GIFs animados a partir de texto ou imagens enviadas pelos usuários. A novidade faz parte do modelo Images 2.6, lançado pela OpenAI, que está disponível globalmente no ChatGPT e no Codex para todos os usuários, incluindo versões para navegador, computador e celulares. A tecnologia também chegou à API para desenvolvedores. Com a atualização, é possível criar GIFs e editar as animações em uma única etapa e sem sair da conversa. Assim, é possível animar mascotes e personagens de marcas, transformar fotos de produtos em sequências que se repetem continuamente, criar storyboards animados e dar movimento a esboços feitos à mão. A interface também oferece controles para alterar a velocidade de reprodução, visualizar os quadros individualmente e editar cenas. A velocidade pode variar de 0,5x a 2x. O Images 2.6 também traz melhorias no desempenho. Segundo a OpenAI, o modelo gera imagens 50% mais rápido do que a versão anterior. A empresa afirma que seus usuários criam mais de 4 bilhões de imagens por semana no ChatGPT, Codex e API. Em setembro, o volume registrado era de 3 bilhões semanais. A atualização também chegou à API da OpenAI , que recebeu duas variantes do modelo. O GPT-Image-2.6 Flare prioriza a velocidade, com geração de imagens em até seis segundos na configuração de baixa qualidade, e foi otimizado para criar pôsteres, fotos de produtos e materiais profissionais com melhor qualidade de layout. Já o GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst oferece maior precisão e consistência, principalmente nas configurações de qualidade média e alta. Além disso, a API ganhou suporte à exportação de arquivos SVG e à marcação de imagens , recurso que já estava disponível no ChatGPT e agora também pode ser usado por desenvolvedores. A OpenAI ainda adicionou parâmetros para controlar a qualidade das imagens e a complexidade do planejamento das cenas. A criação de GIFs acontece na própria conversa com o ChatGPT. É necessário apenas descrever a animação desejada ou enviar uma imagem para servir de referência. Depois da geração, a interface apresenta controles para personalizar o resultado, como: Velocidade : ajuste da reprodução entre 0,5x, 0,75x, 1x, 1,25x, 1,5x, 1,75x e 2x; Visualização dos quadros : abertura de uma tela com a sequência completa de imagens que compõem o GIF; Edição : alteração de detalhes visuais dos quadros; Comentários : inclusão de observações sobre a imagem; Redimensionamento : ajuste das dimensões e da proporção do arquivo; Remoção : exclusão de elementos ou quadros da animação. Quando terminar os ajustes, o usuário pode baixar ou compartilhar o arquivo do GIF. Se você gostou do conteúdo, talvez também se interesse por conferir “ 7 melhores IAs para gerar imagens além do ChatGPT e Gemini ”.

sources.name: MIT Technology Review AI
sources.title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
sources.text: Some of the largest AI infrastructure projects in the world are underway in Texas. A dramatic political shift could slow their construction—and deepen concerns about the economics of the AI boom. Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself. Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether. The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana. The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects. Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it. A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere. It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red. This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices. Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. Surveillance towers, increasingly powered by AI, promised faster responses to crossings. Our investigation of deaths near the towers found they are failing to deliver. Discover special offers, top stories, upcoming events, and more.

sources.name: Fortune
sources.title: Elon Musk spent at least $225 million in Texas. The governor-elect who sued for Abbott emails and vowed a data center freeze won anyway
sources.text: Elon Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets data NPR reported . Texas is home to the headquarters of Tesla and SpaceX, and on Tuesday its voters handed Democrats the governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat, and the state House anyway. Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott , becoming the state’s first Latina governor and ending a Republican hold on the office that began in 1995. James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton , the first Democratic U.S. Senate win in Texas since 1988. Democrats also won control of the Texas House for the first time since Republicans took it in 2002. For Musk, the result replaces a governor who championed his Texas expansion with one who sued to see Abbott’s communications with him and has promised to freeze data center approvals. Tesla, SpaceX, and Terafab, the $16.8 billion chip plant they are building in Grimes County, all depend on state cooperation for their next phase in Texas. Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, PACs, and outside groups this cycle, making him the top donor of the midterms, according to OpenSecrets; other tallies run higher. Since May 2025, he has given more to federal political groups than George Soros has personally given in his lifetime, a Fortune analysis found . Texas hosts Tesla’s Austin headquarters and Gigafactory, SpaceX’s Starbase launch site, and X, which became part of SpaceX when SpaceX merged with xAI in February. Tesla, a Fortune 500 company , is unlikely to see immediate manufacturing disruptions. It could face more scrutiny of its Autopilot and Full Self-Driving technology and its planned Cybercab robotaxi rollout, especially with Democrats also winning both chambers of Congress . Democratic lawmakers could also push for a closer look at Musk’s companies and their government relationships. SpaceX’s Texas expansion and its AI infrastructure ambitions could meet tougher environmental reviews and more contentious debates over electricity, water, and data center development. Hinojosa has made that fight central. “I will issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals,” she said in an Oct. 22 video, pledging to keep it in place until the Legislature passes new protections, the Texas Tribune reported . Abbott himself paused new data center permits in September pending a grid audit. The open question for Musk is how long, and how broadly, a Hinojosa freeze would apply. Terafab’s first phase represents a capital investment of more than $16.8 billion and is expected to create 3,000 jobs, according to Abbott’s office . The full project could be built in up to four phases at a total cost of $55 billion to $119 billion, Manufacturing Dive reported . The state has extended a $30 million Texas Enterprise Fund grant, and the plant qualifies for the Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation (JETI) program, which reduces school property taxes for large projects. The election doesn’t automatically cancel those commitments, but closer scrutiny of incentives and environmental requirements could raise costs or slow later phases. Terafab is a chip plant, not a conventional data center. Its energy and infrastructure demands could still draw attention from officials concerned about industrial expansion, and Musk has said the facility will produce AI chips at scale . Hinojosa challenged Abbott’s relationship with Musk before she won. On Oct. 19, the first day of early voting, she sued for access to unredacted communications between Abbott’s office and Musk and his companies. Her lawsuit says the governor’s office described some of those records as “intimate and embarrassing.” She pointed to a $1.66 billion JETI tax break tied to Terafab , more than $54 million in state grants to SpaceX, and Abbott’s push for the state broadband office to award Starlink $110 million upfront from federal funds, a move that triggered an audit of the office . Abbott’s office called the suit “a baseless stunt.” State District Judge Catherine Mauzy ordered Abbott’s office on Oct. 26 to let Hinojosa inspect the records, and the 15th Court of Appeals stayed that order the next day . Bloomberg Government separately reported that Mauzy had donated $500 to Hinojosa’s campaign in June. Starting in January, Hinojosa will control state appointments, the veto, and the governor’s office that administers the Texas Enterprise Fund. Republicans kept their 19-12 majority in the Texas Senate , but Democrat Vikki Goodwin’s win in the lieutenant governor’s race gives the party the chamber’s presiding officer. Shares of Musk’s two public companies fell the day after the election while the broader market rose. Tesla closed down 3.3% and SpaceX down 3.8% on Nov. 4, according to Yahoo Finance. The timing doesn’t prove investors were reacting to Texas. But Wells Fargo’s chief equity strategist, Ohsung Kwon, had warned that a Democratic win in the governor’s race could be a “left-tail event” for the AI trade, CNBC reported . Musk is also weighing a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, a deal that Democratic majorities in Congress could now scrutinize. Fortune has reported on what the merger talks reveal about his power . Hinojosa takes office in January, the same month lawmakers return to Austin. The next tests are how far her data center freeze reaches, whether Terafab’s JETI agreements draw legislative review, and whether the fight over Abbott’s Musk records outlasts his administration.

stories.title: Experts warn building new data centers across the US could wipe out the last 15 years of greenhouse gas progress
stories.summary: US data centre expansion could increase emissions as gas turbines meet rising demand and renewable generation struggles to keep pace.

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: Experts warn building new data centers across the US could wipe out the last 15 years of greenhouse gas progress
sources.text: New data centres could push US power-sector emissions sharply higher The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure in the United States is creating new concerns about the country's ability to reduce CO 2 emissions. A new Sierra Club assessment warns that electricity generation associated with planned data center developments could reverse years of environmental gains. By 2030, CO 2 emissions linked to the expansion could exceed 460 million metric tons, matching Mexico's annual carbon dioxide emissions. The environmental organisation estimates that electricity demand from proposed facilities could substantially increase pollution from the American power sector before the decade ends. Projections indicate that CO 2 emissions could reach 2.1 billion metric tons, representing a 42% increase over 2025 levels. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” said Jeremy Fusher, Sierra Club's principal advisor for climate and energy, expressing surprise at the scale of the latest estimates. The organisation's earlier calculations placed the projected increase between 25% and 50% of its current estimate. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The revised assessment therefore indicates that electricity requirements associated with planned computing infrastructure could create a huge environmental cost. Natural gas remains an important part of the electricity supply supporting American data centres. Approximately 40% of these facilities receive electricity from gas turbines, while renewable energy additions are struggling to match rapidly increasing consumption. Competition for electricity generation equipment is creating additional difficulties for developers seeking to bring facilities online quickly. Turbine prices have increased by 50%, while manufacturers face substantial production backlogs extending several years. One manufacturer has reportedly opened production reservations for equipment scheduled for delivery in 2032. These constraints could encourage developers to retain fossil fuel generation rather than wait for renewable alternatives or additional electricity infrastructure. Equipment shortages, delayed grid connections and other infrastructure constraints could prevent numerous developments from becoming operational. Across the United States, applications for construction permits reportedly exceed the electricity transmission capacity available in several locations. Some projects also face opposition from communities concerned about electricity consumption, environmental consequences and the costs associated with infrastructure expansion. Financial uncertainty within the artificial intelligence industry introduces another complication for developers planning large computing facilities. Hyperscalers facing questions about the commercial returns from their investments could postpone or abandon projects before construction reaches completion. Government regulations requiring renewable electricity for new facilities may provide some protection against additional emissions. However, existing requirements frequently include implementation periods and generally do not apply retrospectively to operating installations. Ireland, for example, requires new data centres to obtain 80% of their electricity from renewable sources within six years of beginning operations. Such delays mean fossil fuel generation could remain part of the electricity supply during substantial periods of infrastructure expansion. Due to these uncertainties, the eventual impact of data centre expansion on greenhouse gas emissions remains difficult to predict. Efosa has been writing about technology for over 7 years, initially driven by curiosity but now fueled by a strong passion for the field. He holds both a Master's and a PhD in sciences, which provided him with a solid foundation in analytical thinking. sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: After the midterms, a bigger clash over data centers could be coming
sources.text: The November 3 midterm results gave Democrats full control of Congress, setting the stage for what could be one of the most divided U.S. governments this decade, with Republicans in the White House. Tuesday’s results suggest that anger over data centers, the large facilities that house the computers powering AI, is becoming a political force. With Democrats now in control of Congress, that could lead to new limits on where data centers can be built and how much say local communities have. Data centers became a ballot-box issue in various states. An NBC exit poll showed how concerned voters are about AI: More than half of respondents believe that AI will do more harm than good, while almost 80% are against the building of data centers in their neighborhoods. Almost 60%, meanwhile, said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote. Nadine Smith, president and CEO of the racial justice organization Color of Change, called Tuesday’s election a referendum on “who this economy is built for.” “National security matters,” Smith said, referring to a common argument from data center supporters that the infrastructure is essential for the U.S. to stay ahead in war and in its rivalry with China. “And so do the families in South Memphis breathing exhaust from the gas turbines powering an AI supercomputer.” (She was referring to xAI’s data center in Memphis, Tennessee, which uses gas turbines for power.) Voters in several states pushed back against the AI buildout, even as pro-AI super PACs spent millions hoping to sway them this midterm. The anti-data center backlash was especially felt in states like Ohio, where OpenAI has eyed a $500 billion data center, backed by more than $100 billion in financing from Nvidia. In fact, the Ohio county where Meta had planned a 700,000-square-foot facility just passed a ban on data centers, and local communities across the state overwhelmingly voted against data center buildout measures. Analysts at Morgan Stanley predict that Democratic governor-elect Amy Acton will also pose a major risk to Ohio’s data center buildout. Elsewhere, candidates in Texas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Georgia, and South Carolina all won seats after taking a stance against the rapid buildout of data centers. “It is clear that money does not buy outcomes,” said Anshi Bhatt, a tech and policy researcher, adding that in modern politics, creating a “local villain” is one way to build campaign momentum. Likely next steps include more construction moratoriums or requiring data centers to pay for their own power grid upgrades instead of passing those costs on to nearby communities. Goldman Sachs, in fact, predicts data center construction delays in states like Georgia and Texas because of Democratic gains. Democratic control of Congress could also improve the odds for bills like the one Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced earlier this year, though any such bill would also face a possible veto. It proposes a nationwide moratorium on new data centers until Congress adds new guardrails and ensures that the buildout does not raise electricity costs, harm the environment, or proceed without community approval. There are also bills like the GRID Savings Act, proposed by New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, which would prevent grid infrastructure costs from being passed on to communities during large AI data center buildouts. The environment is also a major concern, especially at xAI’s data center in Memphis and at the data centers throughout Virginia, known as the world capital of data centers, where gas turbines are used for power. Maia Woluchem, program director at Data & Society, a nonprofit research group, believes that changes to energy regulations, land rights, and other environmental policies could affect the data center buildout, especially as congressional Democrats look further into the Trump administration’s rollback of certain energy protections, as the New York Times reported they might . “Regardless of federal action, I could imagine that we will see additional movement at the state and local level, given the momentum that’s been building from the ground up,” Woluchem continued, citing governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who supports a statewide moratorium on data centers, as an example. Both Hinojosa and Gov. Greg Abbott called for some limits, but Hinojosa centered much of her campaign on opposing data centers, a notable choice in Texas, whose electrical grid has proved vulnerable over the past decade. But the hard part is still to come. Smith, for example, is now expecting a fight, or even more executive orders, to bypass what Congress is now likely to block. “Even among Democrats, a blanket freeze is contested,” she said, referring to some Democrats’ worry that a moratorium could slow AI progress and hurt national security. She also expects AI lobbyists to start calling lawmakers. “Democrats ran on making Big Tech pay,” Smith said. “Our job is to make sure they remember it once the cameras leave.” The backlash runs deeper than the buildings themselves, which aren’t new. One private equity executive told me recently that people don’t necessarily hate data centers, but rather AI, and that data centers have become a stand-in for people’s fears and anxieties about the technology. “It does look like the results are pointing to a real frustration with tech power at minimum,” Woluchem said, noting that this is also a bipartisan issue. For the past month, people have told me they are worried about data centers’ effect on the environment and about their lack of say in whether they’re built. Amazon, for example, built a data center in Gilroy, California, without many residents knowing , by satisfying a 45-year-old zoning law. Vague or outdated zoning laws, along with requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) barring them from discussing data center projects, have only fueled people’s outrage about the buildout. stories.title: OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke
stories.summary: OpenAI pledged to solicit community input around AI data centers, publish construction plans and protect ratepayers.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke
sources.text: OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI. The artificial intelligence company said in its commitments that for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from using non-disclosure agreements with public officials. Additionally, in a policy blueprint, OpenAI encouraged policymakers to enact similar commitments as laws. "What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward," OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told reporters during a Wednesday briefing. "This will help ensure that there is a very high floor in terms of how people move forward." Other tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic , have outlined several similar commitments . On Tuesday, Americans issued a stinging rebuke of data centers at the polls. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures for all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to AI data centers mounted swiftly over the summer across both sides of the political aisle. Consumers grappling with inflation, rising grocery prices and stubbornly high prices at the pump grew worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, they became a physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy and anxiety around AI. AI companies like OpenAI depend on AI data centers to serve customers and develop new models, and they're seeking to build out as rapidly as possible to meet demand. In February, OpenAI told investors that it's targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and the company has since announced massive data center projects in Georgia and Ohio . OpenAI has repeatedly pledged to protect ratepayers and invest in local communities this year, and Lehane said the company's latest commitments build on many of its previous initiatives. He said the policy blueprint has been in the works since August, and that he met with dozens of lawmakers and candidates since then. "Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance," Lehane said. sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Claude can now analyze your spending with its new Personal Finance tool
sources.text: Anthropic announced Thursday that Claude is getting a new tool called “Personal Finance,” designed to help users keep track of their money. With it, users can connect their bank and credit card accounts through Plaid and ask Claude questions about their finances. Anthropic says access is read-only, meaning Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest users’ money. By letting Claude connect directly to bank and credit card accounts, Anthropic is positioning its chatbot as a financial companion that can help people understand their spending and make sense of their money, rather than simply offering them generic advice. With the launch, Claude is playing catch-up to OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which introduced similar personal finance tools in May that also let users connect their financial accounts and ask questions about everything from spending patterns to long-term financial planning. “Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that’s new to you,” Anthropic wrote in a blog post. “Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer.” For instance, at the end of the month, a user could ask Claude, “Where did my money go this month?” The chatbot will then add up spending across the connected accounts and sort it by category, such as rent and utilities, food and drink, and shopping. Users can choose to go deeper by following up with questions like, “Is that more than usual?” or “Anything else I’m missing?” Anthropic says the tool goes beyond basic spending summaries by analyzing transactions across connected accounts to flag potential issues, such as duplicate charges, unexpected fees, and steadily increasing bills. Users can also ask broader questions about their finances, such as whether they’re spending more than they earn. The tool can also explain financial concepts like APR (annual percentage rate), while providing calculations that show users how much they’ve paid in interest over the past year. Of course, some people will have reservations about connecting their financial accounts to an AI chatbot. Anthropic says Claude’s access is limited to each connected bank’s name, account name and type, the last four digits of the account number, balances, credit limits, and up to two years of transaction history. Additionally, the company notes that when users chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train its models. Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week to users on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the U.S. The launch of the new tool comes as Anthropic has been expanding Claude into new verticals. sources.text: With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.﻿ With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.﻿ Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot “where did my money go this month,” for example, and it’ll create an overview with a breakdown of spending by category, including rent and utilities, shopping, and food. Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month. Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts . Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history. If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions. Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning: “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”
